references.text: The father's own words about slaughtering the fattened calf because the lost son has returned. The servant recounts in verse 27 what the father himself said in Luke 15:23-24.

The Pharisees and the scribes complained that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them. The older brother's reaction mirrors this attitude, and the servant's explanation in verse 27 sets up the contrast. See Luke 15:2.

The same theme of reunion and joy is found in the parable of the lost sheep, where the shepherd calls together friends and neighbors to rejoice. The joy over the son's return reflects this joy; see Luke 15:6-7.

In the parable of the lost coin, the woman celebrates with friends and neighbors when the coin is found. This is the same theme of joy as when the father slaughters the fattened calf; see Luke 15:9-10.
Abraham ran to the herd and fetched a fine, tender calf to prepare a feast for his guests. The slaughter of the fattened calf in the parable recalls this hospitality; see Genesis 18:7.
The woman at En-Dor slaughtered a fattened calf and served it to Saul when he came to her. The fattened calf as a feast meal on special occasions is a recurring theme; see 1 Samuel 28:24-25.

The older brother complains that the father slaughtered the fattened calf for his younger brother. His bitterness stands in sharp contrast to the servant's neutral description in verse 27; see Luke 15:30.
